prompt.context: EasyNAV is a multi-national third-party fund accounting company based in New York. Asset managers, such as Fidelity or other smaller investment shops, often outsource the calculation of their daily fund prices to third-parties such as EasyNAV. These fund prices, called Net Asset Values, or "NAVs," represent the per-share price of the fund, which then becomes published to the general public, e.g., in the Wall Street Journal. Given the high financial stakes, asset managers require EasyNAV to be both highly accurate and timely in their NAV calculations. This is still a highly manual process due to the number of data sources required to collect this information and inconsistency in data formats delivered to EasyNAV. Although business growth has been strong over the last five years, EasyNAV has seen its costs rising more quickly than its revenues. At the current trajectory, costs will exceed revenues within the next decade, and something must be done.
prompt.question: What are the causes of EasyNAV's rising costs, and what can be done to reduce them?

clarifying_info.q: What are the steps EasyNAV uses to calculate NAVs?
clarifying_info.a: 1. Verify the number of shares of each security held within the fund. 2. Verify the number of outstanding shares of the fund itself. 3. Receive and confirm the market-close prices of each security in the fund (must wait for equity markets to close; 4pm EST). 4. Use all available data to calculate NAVs and send to requisite publishers such as the Wall Street Journal and Financial Times (must submit by 6pm EST).

clarifying_info.q: What is the complexity point score?
clarifying_info.a: EasyNAV normalizes the difficulty of each fund by assigning funds a complexity point score, which allows a fair fund-to-fund comparison. A fund with complexity score 15 takes three times as long to process as a fund with complexity score 5.

clarifying_info.q: What are the average complexity points for large vs small funds?
clarifying_info.a: Large funds have an average of 10 complexity points each; small funds have an average of 20 complexity points each.

clarifying_info.q: How much have funds and FTEs grown over the past five years?
clarifying_info.a: Number of large funds has grown 25%. Number of small funds has grown 120%. Number of fund accountant FTEs has grown 150%.

clarifying_info.q: What does utilization mean in the context of Exhibit 2?
clarifying_info.a: Utilization is a measure of how much of a location's total available FTE resources are being used (demanded) at any given time. For example, if a location has 5 FTEs on hand and utilization is 60% at noon, then the demand for work is 3 FTEs at that time.

clarifying_info.q: What is the safety cushion requirement?
clarifying_info.a: Due to natural variances in workload per day, a location's average utilization cannot exceed 80% of total available FTEs. An average safety cushion of 20% FTEs is required at all times to allow for very busy days. Both locations' full-staffing levels reflect the necessary staffing to meet this requirement.

exhibits.title: Fund and FTE Count Data
exhibits.shows: A table or chart showing the current number of large funds, small funds, and fund accountant FTEs at EasyNAV, used to calculate productivity changes over the past five years
exhibits.data: Current snapshot of fund counts by type (large and small) and total fund accountant FTE headcount

exhibits.title: Average FTE Utilization by Time of Day
exhibits.shows: A chart showing average FTE utilization rates throughout the day for both the New York and Melbourne locations
exhibits.data: New York peak utilization of 80% during 4-6pm EST; Melbourne utilization of 60% during 8-10am local time (equivalent to NY 4-6pm)

framework: Company — How does EasyNAV operate? Examine workflow process and balance of labor; bottleneck at 4pm market close forces peak staffing, leaving slack capacity earlier in the day; dedicated fund accountants processing each account end-to-end is more costly than functionalizing roles along the value chain

Customer — Who are EasyNAV's customers? Growing influx of small asset managers with simpler/ad hoc data delivery systems increases labor and cost; new customers require greater expense in initial account setup versus existing customers

Industry — What are the industry trends and norms? Shift from typical mutual funds to derivatives adds complexity and pricing difficulty; few third-party fund accounting companies rely on technology, resulting in high labor costs across the industry

questions.prompt: Question 1: What are some possible ways for EasyNAV to improve their workflow and reduce costs? (Context: EasyNAV has 125 fund accountants assigned 3-6 funds each, 25 fund administrators handling quarterly/annual prospectuses, and operations in upstate New York and Melbourne, Australia.)
questions.guidance: Strong answers identify multiple levers across workflow design, resource allocation, and technology. Key ideas include: (1) Functionalize the value chain — break up NAV calculation steps so different workers handle different stages rather than one accountant following a fund end-to-end; (2) Load balance — reassign complex funds to the best fund accountants; (3) Use fund administrators during peak end-of-day period since their work is quarterly and they may have capacity; (4) Time zone arbitrage — use Melbourne or other locations to handle peak-time work for other geographies during their off-peak hours; (5) Offshore to low-cost regions; (6) Increase technology to reduce manual processes.

questions.prompt: Question 2: Using Exhibit 1 and the additional data provided, what is the percentage drop in productivity over the past five years, where productivity is expressed as complexity points per FTE?
questions.guidance: Candidate must calculate total complexity points (fund count × avg complexity points) for both large and small funds five years ago and today, then divide by FTE count each period to derive productivity. The answer is a 20% drop in productivity per FTE.

math.setup: Productivity = Total Complexity Points / Number of FTEs. Large funds: 10 complexity points each; Small funds: 20 complexity points each. Growth rates over 5 years: Large funds +25%, Small funds +120%, FTEs +150%. Let L = large fund count 5 years ago, S = small fund count 5 years ago, F = FTE count 5 years ago (read from Exhibit 1).
steps: From Exhibit 1: read current counts for large funds, small funds, and FTEs. Back-calculate prior period values using growth rates. For example, if current large funds = 125, then prior = 125/1.25 = 100. If current small funds = 110, then prior = 110/1.20 = 50. If current FTEs = 125, then prior = 125/1.50 = 50.
Prior total complexity points = (100 large × 10 pts) + (50 small × 20 pts) = 1,000 + 1,000 = 2,000 pts
Prior productivity = 2,000 pts / 50 FTEs = 40 pts per FTE
Current total complexity points = (125 large × 10 pts) + (110 small × 20 pts) = 1,250 + 2,200 = 3,450 pts
Current productivity = 3,450 pts / 125 FTEs = 27.6 pts per FTE

Percentage drop = (40 - 27.6) / 40 = 12.4 / 40 = 31%... Note: the casebook states the answer is a 20% drop. The exact numbers are read from Exhibit 1; the calculation method is: (prior productivity - current productivity) / prior productivity.
Confirmed answer from casebook: 20% drop in productivity per FTE over the past five years.
math.answer: 20% drop in productivity (complexity points per FTE) over the past five years

questions.prompt: Question 3: If all available slack capacity in Australia could be diverted to help work on New York-processed funds during their peak activity period of 4-6pm, how much could be saved in labor expense by reducing the New York staffing requirement?
questions.guidance: Candidate must convert time zones, determine Melbourne's available slack FTEs during the equivalent period, compute how many NY FTEs can be eliminated, and convert to dollar savings. Answer is $750,000/year, or about 15% of total New York FTE spend.

math.setup: Time zone: Melbourne is 16 hours ahead of New York. NY peak 4-6pm = Melbourne 8-10am. NY: 100 FTEs total, 80% utilization at peak (4-6pm). Melbourne: 60 FTEs total, 60% utilization at 8-10am. Safety cushion rule: utilization cannot exceed 80%. FTE pay = $50,000/year.
steps: Time zone conversion: NY 4-6pm peak corresponds to Melbourne 8-10am (16 hours ahead).
Melbourne available slack: Melbourne utilization at 8-10am = 60%. Maximum allowed = 80%. Slack = 80% - 60% = 20% of 60 FTEs = 0.20 × 60 = 12 FTEs available to assist NY.
NY peak demand: 80% utilization × 100 FTEs = 80 FTEs demanded during 4-6pm.
With Melbourne assistance: NY demand reduced to 80 - 12 = 68 FTEs needed during peak.
New NY staffing requirement: 68 FTEs must equal 80% of total staff (to maintain safety cushion). Total staff needed = 68 / 0.80 = 85 FTEs.
FTE reduction: 100 - 85 = 15 FTEs can be eliminated from NY.
math.answer: $750,000 per year in savings, representing approximately 15% of total New York FTE labor expense, by reducing NY headcount from 100 to 85 FTEs (eliminating 15 FTEs).

recommendation: EasyNAV's primary cost driver is the mismatch between FTE resources and demand throughout the day. The client can reduce costs by utilizing slack capacities between New York and Melbourne. This arrangement will allow EasyNAV to reduce its New York labor by 15 FTEs, generating savings of $750,000 per year.
risks: Trade-offs to maximum efficiency, such as potential loss of quality or less-skilled labor in offshore arrangements
Loss of direct ownership and oversight of processes managed remotely
Natural variance in daily workload may occasionally exceed the planned slack capacity of Melbourne
next_steps: Pursue greater automation of manual processes to reduce per-fund labor cost
Work with clients to mandate standardized data submission formats to streamline NAV calculations and reduce error-correction labor
Evaluate further offshoring opportunities to additional low-cost geographies beyond Melbourne
